item.title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that "Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)" further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

item.title: Brain extracellular matrix remodelling in health and neuropsychiatric disorders.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
The neural extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as an active regulator of brain function and an important contributor to the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders. This Review examines ECM organization, function and adaptive remodelling in the healthy brain and synthesizes evidence for its pathophysiological alterations in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. Based on findings from human studies and animal models, we propose an ECM-extended conceptual framework of major psychiatric diseases in which polygenic liability, stress exposure and neuroinflammatory signalling converge to remodel the ECM in circuits supporting reward processing, emotion regulation, cognitive control and social cognition. In this model, an early phase of protease-dominant ECM loosening destabilizes microcircuits composed of parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons and principal cells whereas later reactive ECM rebuilding stabilizes dysfunctional network states and contributes to disease persistence, relapse and treatment resistance. This framework positions the ECM as a central hub of genetic, glial, synaptic and systems-level pathogenesis and suggests avenues for the development of ECM-sensitive biomarkers and ECM-directed interventions that may improve the treatment of these disorders.

item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Functions in Patients With Essential Tremor Without Dementia: Beyond the Cerebellum.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Essential tremor (ET) is characterized not only by motor disturbances but also, in many cases, by a wide array of cognitive symptoms. Accumulating evidence implicates pathways beyond the cerebellum by which cognitive changes emerge. However, the extracerebellar neuropathologic correlates of specific cognitive symptoms have not been examined. This study evaluated these potential clinicopathologic associations in older adults with ET. Methods Participants were adults ≥55 years with ET who were followed prospectively and longitudinally and donated their brains for neuropathologic evaluation as part of the Clinical-Pathological Study of Cognitive Impairment in Essential Tremor study. Cognitive outcomes included attention, executive function, language, memory, and visuospatial function. Postmortem neuropathologic assessment included Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque scores, Thal β-amyloid A score, Braak and Braak neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) stage, and Braak Lewy pathology stage. Regional cerebral cortical atrophy ratings (neocortical and hippocampal), cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and markers of cerebrovascular health were also rated. Regression models examined neuropathologic correlates of cognitive function, adjusting for numerous confounders. Sensitivity analyses examined robustness of findings. Results The sample consisted of 57 individuals with ET and without dementia (mean age = 88.6 ± 5.4 years; 54.4% female, 71.9% cognitively normal, 28.1% with mild cognitive impairment). Higher amyloid burden was associated with lower attention (CERAD β = -0.48, p < 0.001; Thal β = -0.37, p < 0.01) and lower executive function (CERAD β = -0.40, p 0.01; Thal β = -0.33, p = 0.01). CERAD score was associated with lower language (β = -0.31, p = 0.04). Braak NFT stage was associated with lower attention (β = -0.26, p = 0.04) and lower executive function (β = -0.28, p = 0.03). Hippocampal atrophy was associated with lower memory performance (β = -0.29, p = 0.04). Discussion Core pathologies of AD, amyloid and tau, are associated with decrements in attention and executive function in older adults with ET and without dementia, while hippocampal atrophy is associated with lower memory performance. These results, consistent with a growing literature on extracerebellar pathologies in ET, suggest that multidomain cognitive symptoms among older adults with ET and without dementia may be driven in large part by AD-related cortical degenerative processes. Ongoing work is examining the molecular basis of these processes. Limitations include a highly educated, demographically homogeneous, and relatively small sample, as well as a lack of a control group.

item.title: The hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine for memory, perception and cognitive dysfunction.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
The hippocampus is a central cognitive hub whose dysfunction contributes to most neurodegenerative dementias. Despite extensive knowledge of its anatomy, physiology and circuitry, a unifying account that links hippocampal dynamics to cognition and clinical syndromes remains lacking. Drawing on systems neuroscience and recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, we conceptualize the hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine that compresses sensory, interoceptive and cognitive inputs into low-dimensional representations and regenerates percepts, episodic memories and imagined scenes for cortical integration. Travelling waves of cortico-hippocampal oscillations, aligned with large-scale functional gradients, schedule and structure this generative process and organize distributed neural activity into coherent, semantically grounded constructs. We formalize this proposal as stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), a biologically grounded framework that maps hippocampal-cortical computations onto specific anatomical substrates and dynamical processes. While we do not suggest that the hippocampus implements diffusion algorithms per se, we show that its computations can be decomposed into homologous operations including compression, stochastic exploration, conditioning and reconstruction, whose formal structure closely parallels that of latent diffusion models. Finally, we demonstrate how major neurodegenerative dementias, including the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia, can be understood as selective breakdowns of distinct components of this generative architecture.

item.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Nature
Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2 . These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

item.title: Remodeling stress-responsive networks following early life adversity: Insights from preclinical models.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup. Preclinical models using primates and rodents have allowed for fine control over these variables, providing substantial evidence of pathways and related biomarkers impacted by ELA. The present review aims to bridge findings from human clinical data with preclinical research, highlighting well-supported ELA-induced changes in the functional connectivity of stress-sensitive pathways, as well as alterations in additional cortical and subcortical pathways which are susceptible to disturbances during development. We also present key neuromodulatory mechanisms contributing to connectivity changes observed in preclinical models, and sex-specific nuances. Addressing these critical gaps could enhance the potential of connectivity-based therapeutic approaches. Lastly, we consider the translatability of functional connectivity analyses using various preclinical techniques for studying the influence of ELA on the developing brain.

item.title: Motor system inefficiency as an activity-dependent amplifier of fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Multiple sclerosis (MS) fatigue is clinically obvious but mechanistically elusive. It can dominate daily life despite modest disability, stable structural MRI findings, or preserved strength on examination. This Update reviews evidence that an important component of MS fatigue may arise from increased motor-control cost and incomplete recovery after activity. Voluntary muscle activation studies show that some people with MS have incomplete central access to available force, particularly after exertion. Functional imaging studies indicate that apparently preserved movement often depends on expanded recruitment of premotor, cerebellar, striatal, prefrontal, and cingulo-insular systems involved in motor compensation, effort allocation, and body-state monitoring. Metabolic and pathological studies further indicate energetic vulnerability in demyelinated and chronically injured networks, providing biological plausibility for impaired restoration after repeated signalling demands. These findings support a systems framework in which expanded motor-control recruitment may be compensatory when it preserves performance and remains flexible and recoverable, but may amplify MS fatigue when ordinary activity begins from incompletely restored physiological reserve. We outline testable predictions for identifying a motor-cost fatigue phenotype and for designing repeated-measures studies of activity-related fatigue in MS.

item.title: Chronic and subacute phenylalanine effects on brain metabolism in adults with phenylketonuria.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Phenylketonuria (PKU) leads to chronic cerebral exposure to elevated phenylalanine (Phe) despite lifelong dietary treatment, yet the neurometabolic consequences in adulthood remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent alterations in brain metabolism and whether these metabolites respond dynamically to subacute Phe fluctuations. Adults with early-treated PKU (n=30) and healthy controls (n=59) underwent proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS), structural and functional brain MRI to evaluate white matter lesion load (T2-weighted images) and cerebral blood flow (arterial spin labeling), as well as cognitive assessments. Patients additionally participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover intervention with four weeks of oral Phe loading to evaluate subacute metabolic responsiveness. Absolute metabolite concentrations were quantified in predominantly white matter tissue, and associations between blood and brain Phe, white matter lesion load, cerebral blood flow, and cognitive performance were examined. At baseline, patients exhibited higher brain Phe and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) levels, alongside reduced myo-inositol, N-acetylaspartylglutamate (NAAG), and total creatine/phosphocreatine compared with controls. Patients with white matter lesions did not differ in blood and brain metabolites from those without. Four weeks of oral Phe loading increased brain Phe and produced a reversible decrease in myo-inositol, whereas NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds remained unchanged. Blood and brain Phe concentrations were strongly correlated (r=0.83, p<0.001), and their ratio was subject-dependent. No significant associations were observed between metabolite concentrations and regional cerebral blood flow or cognitive performance after correction for multiple comparisons. Adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent neurometabolic alterations involving neuronal-glial metabolism, energy buffering, and astrocytic osmolyte regulation. The findings support a trait-state framework, with stable alterations in NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds reflecting long-standing metabolic changes, superimposed on a dynamically Phe-sensitive astrocytic response indexed by myo-inositol. The absence of strong associations with cerebral perfusion or cognition suggests that these alterations represent upstream biological processes not captured by macroscopic imaging or behavioral measures.

item.title: Frequency-Specific Thalamocortical Network Dynamics During Focal Seizures in Humans.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives The thalamus is an emerging neuromodulation target in drug-resistant focal epilepsy because of its frequent ictal involvement. However, frequency-specific and directional thalamocortical dynamics remain poorly understood. We sought to characterize thalamocortical network dynamics across seizure evolution using stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). Methods We retrospectively analyzed SEEG recordings from patients with pediatric-onset drug-resistant focal epilepsy with simultaneous cortical and thalamic sampling focusing on the anterior nucleus (AN) and centromedian nucleus (CM). We applied visual analysis with quantitative measures of spectral power, imaginary coherence, and spectral Granger causality across slow (1-12 Hz), β (13-30 Hz), and γ (30-70 Hz) bands to quantify thalamocortical and cortico-cortical interactions from seizure onset to termination. Random forest models were trained to classify seizure state using thalamic EEG features as an exploratory analysis. Results The final cohort comprised 19 patients (median age, 16.9 years; 31.6% female), with 66 focal seizures analyzed. Thalamic ictal activity was present at seizure onset in 81% of sampled thalamic contacts and became nearly universal by seizure termination. Both the thalamus and seizure onset zone showed increased spectral power during seizures, with prominent slow-band augmentation at seizure termination in the thalamus. Similarly, thalamocortical imaginary coherence increased during seizures, with the largest changes near seizure termination in the slow band (AN-SOZ: 11% [IQR, 2 to 20], rank-biserial correlations (rrb) = 0.84; CM-SOZ: 12% [IQR, 3 to 23], rrb = 0.84) and β band (AN-SOZ: 5% [IQR, 0 to 12], rrb = 0.74; CM-SOZ: 8% [IQR, 2 to 15], rrb = 0.86). Directed connectivity analyses demonstrated bidirectional thalamocortical interactions, with large slow-frequency thalamus-to-SOZ outflow near seizure termination from both AN and CM, exceeding propagation-zone-to-SOZ cortico-cortical flow (both p < 0.01). Seizure state was classified using thalamic EEG features, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.825 for AN and 0.839 for CM. Discussion Human focal seizures engage frequency-specific and bidirectional thalamocortical interactions that evolve from onset to termination. These findings support the thalamus as a source of clinically relevant seizure-state information and may inform thalamic biomarker development for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy.

item.title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neandertal crania were less globular than those of modern humans, suggesting differences in the relative volumes of brain regions, including the frontal and occipital lobes. Here, we show that a common genetic variant influencing occipital brain volume in present-day people was inherited from Neandertals. The variant lies in predicted transcription-factor recognition motifs near DAAM1 , a gene that is known to be involved in brain development. Carriers of the Neandertal variant have altered DAAM1 expression and occipital lobe volumes that are about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. The variant is associated with reduced schizophrenia risk by almost 10% in homozygous carriers, while Neandertal ancestry as a whole does not show such a tendency. Any association with cognition or schooling is small or nonexistent, amounting to at most two weeks of education per allele against an average of about 15 y. Thus, this Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability.

item.title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5-20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

item.title: Spatial coupling between anosmia-related cortical alterations and regional gene expression: an imaging transcriptomics study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background The impact of anosmia on brain cortical structure and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated causal associations between anosmia and cortical alterations using a multi-modal approach combining neuroimaging and genetics. Methods High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging was acquired from 52 patients with anosmia and 50 healthy controls to extract cortical surface area (SA) and cortical thickness (TH). Mendelian randomization (MR) was employed to assess the causal effect of anosmia on cortical structure using summary statistics from the ENIGMA consortium. Furthermore, integrating gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), partial least squares regression (PLSR) and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) were used to identify genes associated with changes in SA and TH due to anosmia. Gene enrichment analysis and cell type-specific analysis were then performed to explore the potential molecular mechanisms. Results Patients exhibited significantly reduced SA in the left rostral anterior cingulate and superior temporal sulcus, while TH was increased in regions including the left cuneus and supramarginal gyrus. MR analysis identified 11 cortical structural features nominally associated with anosmia, although none survived multiple comparison correction across 138 tests. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes correlated with these structural alterations, which were significantly enriched in synaptic pathways (e.g., postsynaptic membrane modulation) and specifically implicated GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. Conclusion Anosmia is causally associated with distinct cortical structural alterations. These regional changes are spatially coupled with molecular signatures involving synaptic function and neuronal plasticity, providing novel insights into the potential pathophysiology of olfactory loss.

item.title: The disrupted navigational compass: pathophysiological mechanisms and clinical interventions for spatial navigation deficits.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Spatial navigation is a higher-order integrative cognitive ability that supports environmental orientation, goal-directed route selection, and adaptive locomotion by integrating spatial memory, multisensory cues, attention, and executive control. Neural systems supporting navigation are also vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease, making navigation a useful domain for linking basic mechanisms with clinically measurable functional impairment. This review summarizes spatial-navigation mechanisms across multiple levels. At the cognitive level, navigation depends on interacting processes including spatial representation, path integration, reference-frame transformation, landmark use, and route planning. At the network level, hippocampal-entorhinal, retrosplenial-parietal, scene-selective, and prefrontal systems contribute complementary functions. At the cellular level, place-, grid-, head-direction-, speed-, and boundary-related representations encode position, heading, self-motion, environmental geometry, and prospective behavior. Clinical and neuroimaging studies indicate that navigation impairment is associated with structural and functional abnormalities, with the strongest diagnostic evidence currently arising from Alzheimer's disease and its prodromal stages. VR-based behavioral assessment and electrophysiological approaches provide complementary means of characterizing navigation phenotypes: VR enables controlled, repeatable, process-sensitive tasks, whereas intracranial and scalp recordings provide neural information at different spatial and physiological scales. No pharmacological agent has been developed or licensed specifically for navigation impairment; current navigation-focused interventions therefore rely mainly on behavioral and VR-based rehabilitation, compensatory strategies, and emerging neuromodulation approaches. Future studies should integrate process-specific behavioral and physiological markers with biomarker-defined clinical cohorts, and use large, randomized, longitudinal studies to establish diagnostic validity, real-world transfer, and mechanism-informed intervention effects.

item.title: Associations between white matter network alterations and visuospatial and social-emotional deficits in patients with right hemisphere tumors: a prospective clinico-radiological study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Preserving neurological function is crucial in brain tumor surgery. Because the right hemisphere supports visuospatial and social‑cognitive abilities, damage may affect quality of life. This prospective study (TANGO; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04288505) examined associations between visuospatial and social‑emotional deficits and tractography‑based white matter alterations in patients with right hemisphere tumors. Thirty‑four patients were assessed preoperatively and 22 postoperatively using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and four neuropsychological tests. Tractography metrics were extracted for nine right hemisphere tracts. Thirty‑four Human Connectome Project participants served as controls. Preoperatively, deficits in visuospatial functioning, facial emotion recognition, and mentalizing were associated with predominantly right hemisphere microstructural abnormalities within distributed white matter networks. Visuospatial deficits were associated with alterations involving the frontal aslant tract (FAT), arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), and SLF II; facial emotion recognition deficits with the SLF III and uncinate fasciculus (UF); and mentalizing deficits with the AF. Postoperatively, exploratory findings suggested associations between new social-emotional deficits and structural alterations involving the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), SLF, and SLF III, whereas new visuospatial deficits showed a trend toward reduced right FAT volume. Relative to controls, left hemisphere tractographic changes were observed regardless of the presence of visuospatial and/or social-emotional deficits, whereas right hemisphere alterations were primarily observed in patients with such deficits. These findings highlight the role of right hemisphere networks in supporting visuospatial and social-emotional functioning. Further characterization of white matter connectivity may help improve risk stratification, surgical planning, and rehabilitation strategies.

item.title: Fixel-based analysis identifies selective vulnerability of non-dominant fiber populations in aging and mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Fixel-based analysis (FBA) resolves fiber-specific white matter properties within crossing-fiber regions, where conventional diffusion tensor imaging is limited. We applied single-shell three-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution to diffusion MRI from 295 older adults in the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project cohort, quantifying fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their composite (FDC) across the primary (N1), secondary (N2), and tertiary (N3) fiber populations within each white matter voxel. White matter was stratified into crossing-fiber complexity strata defined by the number of distinct bundles per voxel, and covariate-adjusted models examined associations with age, cognitive status, and cognition. FC declined with age most steeply in the non-dominant fiber populations. In these populations, FC was lower in participants with mild cognitive impairment than in cognitively unimpaired participants, and higher FC was associated with better executive function. The age-related decline in non-dominant FC did not vary across crossing-fiber complexity, indicating that fiber-population identity, rather than local architecture, organizes age-related vulnerability. FD and FDC showed age associations that became more positive as complexity increased, with the N1 FD association reversing from negative in the least complex regions to positive in the most complex. This behavior is consistent with how density is estimated in multi-fiber voxels rather than with fiber loss, identifying FC as the more interpretable metric in crossing-fiber regions. These findings identify fiber cross-section in the non-dominant fiber populations as a sensitive marker of white matter aging and cognitive status and provide a framework for fiber-specific analysis in existing single-shell cohorts.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: The neuroscience of delirium: a perfect storm for acute brain dysfunction.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Delirium is a frequent and distressing neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by acute disturbances of attention, awareness and cognition. Delirium emerges in response to diverse medical insults, particularly in hospitalized patients. Despite its high prevalence and association with accelerated cognitive decline, dementia and mortality, the neurobiology of delirium remains incompletely understood, and there are no treatments for delirium. Evidence from electrophysiology, neuroimaging, biomarkers and emerging animal models has begun to clarify the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying delirium. Delirium can be conceptualized as the interaction of acute systemic or cerebral stressors with pre-existing vulnerabilities, creating a 'perfect storm' for brain dysfunction. Generalized electroencephalographic slowing and network disintegration are convergent signatures across diverse types of delirium. Disruptions in neuromodulatory systems, energy metabolism and neuroimmune signalling may underlie impairment of large-scale brain function. The mechanisms that drive acute delirium may also contribute to subsequent brain injury and long-term decline, compounding its broad personal and societal impact.

item.title: Alpha coherence is a network signature of cognitive recovery from disorders of consciousness.
item.description:
Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
Alpha (8-12 Hz) frequency band oscillations are among the most informative features in electroencephalographic (EEG) assessment of patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC). Because interareal alpha synchrony is thought to facilitate long-range communication in healthy brains, coherence measures of resting-state alpha oscillations may provide insights into a patient's capacity for higher-order cognition beyond channel-wise estimates of alpha power. In multi-channel EEG, global coherence methods may be used to augment standard spectral analysis methods by assessing both the strength and spatiotemporal structure of coherent oscillatory networks. We performed global coherence analysis in 95 separate clinical EEG recordings (28 healthy controls and 33 patients with acute or chronic DoC, 25 of whom returned for follow-up) collected between two academic medical centers. We found that posterior alpha coherence is associated with recovery of cognitive status represented by a CRS-R total score of 22 or above. We developed a measure of network organization based on the principal eigenvector of the cross-spectral matrix in the alpha band. This network measure performs well in classifying recovery from DoC (AUC = .78) compared to measures of functional connectivity based on the weighted phase lag index (AUC = .45 - .53). Our findings suggest that normalization of network activity in the alpha band may represent a sensitive signature of cognitive recovery in patients with DoC and that network-based methods may augment the utility of EEG assessments for DoC.

item.title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

item.title: Microstructural alterations of human medial temporal lobe in dementia: volumetric and DTI findings correlate with cell number and neuropathology.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Volumetric and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) alterations in medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions are consistently reported in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, their biological basis remains poorly understood. We combined Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) metrics with cellular quantification and neuropathological burden assessment to investigate microstructural substrates underlying MTL imaging alterations in human donors with known cognitive and neuropathological status. Absolute cell numbers were quantified in a cohort of 54 brain donors using the isotropic fractionator, and postmortem MRI was performed on a subset of 18 fixed brain hemispheres. To assess microstructural brain alterations associated with disease progression, in vivo volumetric and DTI metrics were analyzed in 39 cognitively unimpaired controls (CU), 31 individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 14 patients with clinical AD dementia. In the postmortem cohort, MTL diffusivity metrics showed moderate negative correlations with total cell numbers. Mean, axial, and radial diffusivity positively correlated with Braak stage, whereas fractional anisotropy (FA) correlated negatively with CERAD score, linking diffusion alterations to AD-related pathology. In vivo MTL analyses revealed increased mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, and reduced FA in AD patients compared with both CU and MCI individuals. The MCI group exhibited intermediate alterations in diffusivity. Differences between in vivo and postmortem diffusion values were consistent with tissue fixation, temperature, and variations in acquisition protocols. Our findings suggest that diffusion MRI alterations in the MTL are associated with reduced cellularity and neuropathological burden, supporting the biological relevance of DTI metrics as markers of microstructural degeneration in AD.

item.title: Convergent and divergent neural signatures of cue-induced response in substance and behavioral addictions: A coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Addiction-related cues trigger craving and precipitate relapse, yet whether substance use disorders (SUDs) and behavioral addictions (BAs) share a universal neurobiological cue-reactivity core remains unresolved. We conducted a coordinate-based meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI) to synthesize whole-brain fMRI studies comparing visually evoked cue-reactivity in strictly diagnosed SUDs and BAs versus healthy controls. An updated systematic search through September 12, 2026, yielded 50 eligible articles comprising 53 independent contrasts and 2578 participants. Pooled analyses across all addictions revealed convergent cue-elicited activations in the mid-cingulate cortex, precentral gyrus, and a midline midbrain region. However, a formal SUD ∩ BA conjunction analysis yielded no family-wise error (FWE)-corrected shared clusters. Direct comparisons demonstrated greater activation in the left hippocampus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus for SUDs relative to BAs. Importantly, the left hippocampal and precuneus differences survived age adjustment; furthermore, the hippocampal finding remained robust when restricting analyses to highly controlled cue-versus-neutral paradigms, while the precuneus finding was retained within picture-cue modalities. Furthermore, exploratory analyses of clinical characteristics indicated that cue-elicited neural responses were associated with specific clinical states and treatment variables (e.g., methadone maintenance in heroin use disorder), highlighting the modulatory effect of clinical symptom profiles on these regional functional signatures. Overall, the results motivate further investigation of memory- and self-related processes, as well as control- or action-related processes. These findings offer a critical foundation for developing targeted clinical interventions, distinguishing between generalized transdiagnostic neuromodulation targets and disorder-specific therapies tailored to distinct clinical and demographic profile.

item.title: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.

item.title: Hormonal Effects during the Reproductive Years on Brain and Behavior: Molecular Discovery to Promising Therapeutics for Women's Mental Health.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Beginning at puberty and throughout the lifespan, women experience greater rates of depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and hormone-linked mood disorders relative to men. How these disorders relate to hormonal fluctuations and associated changes in physiology and brain circuitry in women during the reproductive years is only partially understood. In this review, the molecular, structural, and functional brain changes during the reproductive years are discussed, with a specific focus on transitional changes during the perinatal period. Preclinical and clinical models of neuroplastic change are also discussed, along with neuromodulatory approaches that account for the contextual, spatial, and temporal parameters of interventions delivered during the postpartum period. Future directions may consider how hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years may improve preclinical and clinical models for women's mental health while acknowledging that greater work is needed to understand the role of a broader range of hormonal and environmental factors linked to mental health including lactation, trauma, contraceptive use, menstruation, and perimenopause.

item.title: Hidden Vision and Beyond: Multiscale Foundations of Thalamic Organization.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The subcortical visual system is traditionally described through a small number of canonical pathways, with the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) viewed primarily as a first-order relay to primary visual cortex and additional routes through the superior colliculus, pulvinar and koniocellular LGN considered secondary or residual. Here, we review recent evidence across species, methods, and scales that challenge this framework and suggest that the visual thalamus is an active, dynamically regulated component of visual processing. We first consider primary and nonprimary visual pathways, showing how thalamic inputs shape cortical responses through the timing, spatial arrangement, synaptic organization, laminar targeting, and circuit-level integration of feedforward signals. We then reconsider the "first-order" status of LGN itself, reviewing evidence that nonretinal subcortical inputs, local inhibition, and corticothalamic feedback can alter LGN responses and the signals routed onward to cortex. This shifts the view of LGN from a passive relay supplying a dynamic cortex to a dynamically regulated node in its own right. Next, we review advances in higher-order thalamic organization, highlighting structured thalamocortical connectivity, network-level coordination, and state-dependent dynamics. Finally, we consider how thalamic functions change in the injured brain, where emerging models disentangle acute effects of damage from chronic compensation to reveal how surviving thalamic and downstream pathways may be remodeled, reweighted, or recruited to support residual visual function and recovery. Together, these findings support a multiscale view of the thalamus as a collection of specialized, adaptive nuclei embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical networks, with implications for perception, cognition, sensory disorders, and rehabilitation.

item.title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched input-output modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.

item.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. Methods In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. Results Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). Semantic processing was highly specific but insensitive for predicting both recovery of consciousness (specificity 94%, sensitivity 18%) and functional recovery (specificity 92%, sensitivity 29%). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. Discussion EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

item.title: Insight discordance differentiates behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia from false positives.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) can present with behavioural symptoms similar to psychiatric mimics of the disease (sometimes termed 'phenocopies'). Despite this overlap, loss of insight is a cardinal feature of bvFTD unlike most psychiatric disorders. This study tested whether insight could be quantified to improve diagnostic accuracy in distinguishing these conditions, and examined neuroimaging correlates of impaired insight. In this prospective cohort study, 27 patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) presenting as the bvFTD phenotype and 25 false-positives of bvFTD who ultimately had a psychiatric disorder underwent patient, informant, and clinician symptom ratings on a modified Frontal Behavioural Inventory (FBI). Discrepancy scores were calculated, diagnostic discrimination was evaluated by area under the curve (AUC) with leave-one-out cross-validation, alongside a neuroimaging analysis of network-level associations of insight in bvFTD. Patients with bvFTD endorsed fewer symptoms than false-positives (FBI 6.62 ± 8.80 vs 15.36 ± 8.42, P < 0.001), whereas clinician observations were markedly greater in bvFTD (27.67 ± 8.35 vs 5.64 ± 3.85, P < 0.001). Informant ratings did not differ between groups (25.15 ± 11.11 vs 21.32 ± 12.61, P = 0.14), even though bvFTD informants had more knowledge of the disease (FTD Knowledge Scale 16.20 ± 6.68 vs 9.41 ± 8.19, P = 0.003). A model incorporating patient-clinician and informant-clinician discrepancy showed excellent cross-validated discrimination (AUC 0.99, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.97-1.00). A model independent of expert clinician ratings, the patient-informant discrepancy, showed fair cross-validated discrimination across the full cohort (AUC 0.71, 95% CI 0.56-0.85) and good discrimination in those who did not develop another FTLD syndrome on follow-up ('pure bvFTD'; AUC 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.94). In bvFTD, reduced insight was associated with salience and semantic appraisal network degeneration but not control frontotemporal regions. BvFTD, false-positives, and their informants demonstrated opposing patterns of symptom endorsement. Symptom under-endorsement (lack of insight) by patients relative to clinician and informant observation supports neurodegeneration, whereas informant and patient over-endorsement without clinician-observed disturbance suggests a false-positive. Unfamiliarity with bvFTD may contribute to over-reporting. Though the clinician-dependent findings may not translate to non-expert settings, the patient-informant model retained good discrimination. Formal quantification of discrepancy patterns in behaviour may reduce misdiagnosis in bvFTD. The neuroimaging findings support salience and semantic appraisal networks as the neuroanatomical basis for insight in bvFTD. Future studies should validate the FBI clinician version and examine factors underlying over-reporting by false-positives and their informants.

item.title: Mosaic CDKL5 deficiency drives progressive inhibitory circuit remodelling.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
CDKL5 deficiency disorder predominantly affects heterozygous females, in whom random X-chromosome inactivation generates cellular CDKL5 mosaicism. Although mosaicism is a defining feature of the disease, whether it actively drives disease progression or simply reflects the genetic mode of inheritance remains unknown. Here, we combined age-comparative electrophysiology, quantitative synaptic imaging, transcriptomic profiling and postmortem human brain analyses to determine how mosaic CDKL5 deficiency shapes inhibitory circuit remodeling during disease progression. Heterozygous Cdkl5 female mice exhibited striking age- and region-specific remodeling of inhibitory neurotransmission. Hippocampal inhibition was initially enhanced but progressively declined with age, whereas cortical inhibitory transmission remained preserved at 3 months and increased in middle-aged animals. These functional changes were accompanied by dynamic remodeling of inhibitory presynaptic terminals, persistent disruption of inhibitory synapse organization and reduced hippocampal gephyrin-positive puncta despite preservation of the major inhibitory interneuron populations. At 12 months, heterozygous females also exhibited a higher density of IBA1/CD68 double-positive microglia in both regions compared with age-matched wild-type controls. Importantly, complete Cdkl5 deficiency failed to reproduce the progressive loss of inhibitory presynaptic terminals observed in heterozygous females, indicating that this phenotype is specific to the mosaic condition rather than a simple consequence of complete Cdkl5 loss. Transcriptomic profiling revealed a temporal transition from alterations detected at 3 months in immune-synaptic regulatory pathways to activity-dependent transcriptional programs associated with reduced structural and homeostatic support, consistent with progressive hippocampal circuit reorganization. Exploratory analyses of postmortem cortical tissue from individuals with CDD revealed differences in inhibitory presynaptic labeling between the available young and adult cases, suggesting that inhibitory alterations may also vary with age in human CDD. Together, these findings identify mosaic CDKL5 deficiency as a biologically distinct circuit state characterized by progressive, region-specific inhibitory circuit remodeling and provide a mechanistic framework for disease progression in CDKL5 deficiency disorder.

item.title: Transdiagnostic variation in age-related patterns of rich-club organization across neurodevelopmental and related mental health conditions.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Rich-club organization is a topographical property of functional brain networks where highly connected regions are more densely interconnected. The rich-club has been shown to be vital for supporting cognitive functioning, and differences have been associated with a wide range of mental health and developmental conditions. This type of organization undergoes complex changes across development, and we have previously shown that males and females have strikingly distinct age-related changes. While disruptions in its development have been related to neurodevelopmental conditions and related mental health conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), the diagnostic- and sex-specific age-related patterns remain unexplored. These conditions also have heterogeneous and overlapping neurobiology and phenotype, and thus transdiagnostic approaches may be most suitable for addressing the complexities. Here, we combine the temporal advantages of magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a data-driven, transdiagnostic approach to parse the heterogeneity of age-related variation in rich-club organization in 386 neurodivergent (116 ADHD, 231 autism, 39 OCD) and 231 neurotypical children and youth, stratified by biological sex. In males and females, subgroups with distinct age-related patterns of rich-club organization did not align cleanly with the diagnostic categories. These patterns were frequency specific, separating the female subgroups in the alpha and gamma bands and the male subgroups in the theta, alpha, beta, and high gamma bands. While the female subgroups differed in their proportions of autistic and neurotypical individuals, all diagnostic categories were represented across the subgroups. The female subgroups also differed in intelligence, while the male subgroups differed in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. Together, our findings indicate that frequency-specific, age-related variation in rich-club organization is largely shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children and youth, rather than delineating diagnostic categories, and highlight the importance of considering sex when studying the biological constructs underlying neurodivergence.

item.title: Load-dependent brain network reconfiguration deficits in childhood ADHD revealed by source-space MEG and Graph Transformer modeling.
item.description:
Developmental cognitive neuroscience
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is clinically heterogeneous, motivating biomarkers that capture how brain networks reorganize under cognitive demand. We studied 122 children aged 8-12 years (61 with ADHD and 61 controls) during a visually cued attention/inhibition paradigm spanning three operationalized composite demand levels in whole-head MEG; structural MRI supported anatomical source modeling, and 34 children with ADHD completed approximately 6 months of follow-up. After denoising, head-motion compensation, ICA-based artifact removal, dSPM source reconstruction, and Morlet wavelet decomposition, we extracted source time series from 68 DKT cortical regions, quantified dynamic connectivity with PLV, wPLI, AEC, and MI, derived graph-theoretic and hidden Markov model features, and trained a spatiotemporal Graph Transformer. Behavioral group differences increased with cognitive demand, with high-load accuracy showing a large effect size (d=1.71). Relative to controls, children with ADHD showed weaker frontoparietal θ coupling, stronger default-mode α coupling, reduced occupancy of frontoparietal-dominant states, greater default-mode state persistence, lower global efficiency, higher modularity, and smaller gains in network flexibility; frontoparietal flexibility showed the strongest association with inattentive symptoms (rs =-0.78). Under participant-level nested cross-validation, the Graph Transformer achieved 94.3% accuracy for three-class cognitive-demand classification (AUC = 0.981) and 96.7% accuracy for ADHD diagnosis (AUC = 0.991). Secondary presentation analyses reached 83.6% accuracy (95% CI: 73.8%-91.8%), and higher baseline frontoparietal flexibility in the follow-up subset was associated with subsequent medication response (OR = 8.49, 95% CI: 2.31-31.2). In an independent task-matched MEG cohort (n=45), zero-shot ADHD diagnostic accuracy was 90.0% (AUC = 0.952), increasing to 94.2% (AUC = 0.981) after limited classification-head adaptation on a separate subset. Together, these results identify load-dependent network flexibility and state-transition measures as candidate adjunctive biomarkers and define prospective multi-center validation as the next translational test.

item.title: Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.

item.title: When defense becomes compulsion: An evolutionary and circuit framework for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors that are frequently organized around preventing potential harm. Although existing neurobiological models have focused on abnormalities in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, habit formation, and cognitive control, they provide a less complete explanation for why compulsions preferentially take the form of precautionary actions. Here, we propose an evolutionary and circuit-level framework in which compulsive behavior is understood as a pathological dysregulation of neural systems that normally support adaptive defense. Integrating evidence from human studies with circuit-level findings from rodent studies, we organize defensive control into three sequential but interacting stages: threat appraisal, defensive action selection and execution, and post-defense safety assessment. During threat appraisal, abnormalities in sensory salience, threat valuation, contextual gating, and interoceptive processing may increase the salience or threat value of ambiguous cues. During action selection and execution, intolerance of uncertainty, impaired behavioral flexibility, corticostriatal dysfunction, and negative reinforcement may bias behavior toward premature and repetitive threat-reducing actions that can become increasingly habitual. Following defensive action, impaired outcome evaluation and safety-state updating may prevent successful actions from generating stable signals of safety or completion, allowing defensive responding to persist despite objective threat reduction. By organizing OCD-related circuitry according to when it contributes to defensive processing rather than solely where abnormalities occur, this framework integrates threat-based, corticostriatal, habit, and safety-learning accounts into a process-based model of how adaptive defense may transition into persistent compulsive behavior. This framework may help map stage-specific dysfunction onto symptom heterogeneity and guide more targeted interventions.

item.title: The separation-distress network as a transdiagnostic mechanism linking relational adversity, social pain, and psychopathology.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Relational trauma is a major contributor to the development of mental health disorders. This association likely reflects the social nature of humans and other mammals, whose survival depends on maintaining stable social bonds. When these bonds are threatened or disrupted, individuals experience social pain, a distress response mediated by the mammalian separation-distress network. During early development, this network is sensitive to maintaining proximity with caregivers, as independent survival is not yet possible. Converging evidence from ethology, psychodynamic and attachment theory, and social and affective neuroscience supports the function of this network. Because mammalian brains are inherently tuned to form social bonds, adverse relational experiences can disrupt socioemotional development and increase vulnerability to psychopathology. Neural substrates of separation distress include the anterior cingulate cortex, ventral septum, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, dorsal preoptic area, dorsomedial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, with endogenous opioids and glucocorticoids serving as key neurochemical modulators in the separation-distress response. Separation distress and adverse relational experiences also alter physiological systems implicated in psychopathology, including the HPA axis, autonomic nervous system activity, inflammation, and brain structure and connectivity. This paper argues that relational trauma and social pain are mediated by an evolutionarily conserved subcortical separation-distress network shared across predominantly mammalian species. Dysregulation of this network may represent one common mechanism underlying depression, social anxiety, suicidality, substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Understanding the processes linking adverse relational experiences, separation-distress activation, and social pain may provide insights into the etiology and treatment of diverse disorders.

item.title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

item.title: Altered interhemispheric functional cooperation in persistent postural-perceptual dizziness.
item.description:
Frontiers in neurology
BACKGROUND: Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) is associated with altered multisensory processing, but its hemispheric functional organization remains poorly understood. We investigated hemispheric functional lateralization and interhemispheric cooperation in PPPD and explored their associations with clinical symptoms and neurotransmitter density maps. METHODS: A total of 47 patients with PPPD and 52 healthy controls (HCs) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Whole-brain maps of the autonomy index (AI) and connectivity between functionally homotopic voxels (CFH) were generated. Between-group differences were assessed using permutation-based analyses adjusted for age, sex, and mean framewise displacement (FD). Associations with clinical measures and spatial correspondence with 13 neurotransmitter density maps were also examined. RESULTS: The PPPD and HC groups did not differ significantly in age, sex, or educational level (all p > 0.05). Patients with PPPD had lower MoCA-BJ scores and higher HAMA-14, HAMD-24, PSQI, and DHI scores than HCs, whereas MMSE scores did not differ significantly. No between-group differences in AI survived family-wise error (FWE) correction. By contrast, in the primary analysis, patients with PPPD showed significantly reduced CFH in the right calcarine cortex, right cuneus, left inferior and middle occipital gyri, left inferior parietal lobule, and right middle temporal gyrus. However, no CFH clusters survived cluster-level FWE correction after separately adjusting for HAMA-14, HAMD-24, or PSQI scores. After adjustment for age, sex, and mean FD, CFH in the right calcarine cortex and left inferior parietal lobule showed negative associations with DHI total and DHI-E scores, respectively (Shepherd's π = -0.363 and -0.452), but neither association remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The CFH group-difference map showed nominal positive spatial correlations with the D2R and VAChT density maps, but these associations were not significant after FDR correction. CONCLUSION: In primary analysis, PPPD patients exhibited reduced interhemispheric functional cooperation in visual, visuospatial and multisensory regions, while no AI differences survived FWE correction. However, these CFH findings were sensitive to adjustment for affective symptoms and sleep quality; the relative contributions of PPPD, affective symptoms and sleep disturbance remain uncertain. Clinical and neurotransmitter density-map associations did not survive FDR correction and are exploratory.

item.title: Brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression: Desynchronization between salience network neuropsychological connectivity and heart rate variability.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Somatic depression is a distinct subtype of major depressive disorder, with a poorer response to treatment, an elevated risk of suicidal behaviour, and a worse prognosis. Interoception, the sense of internal bodily signals, is related to somatic symptoms. However, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of body brain communication remain unclear. 293 depressed patients (145 with somatic symptoms and 148 without), and 160 healthy controls underwent magnetoencephalography during a resting state. Both the intra- and inter-network neural oscillation patterns of the salience network, were computed, alongside and heart rate variability (HRV) as a measure of autonomic function. Individuals with somatic depression exhibited lower HRV, accompanied by theta hyper-connectivity within the salience network. Although higher theta connectivity was linked to increased HRV in controls, this correlation was attenuated or even reversed in patients with somatic depression. Our findings identify a specific pattern of brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression, characterized by disrupted communication between salience network theta oscillations and autonomic cardiac regulation. This provides novel neuroimaging evidence for body-brain communication deficits in a clinically important depression subtype.

item.title: Mapping Individual Brain Deviations in ICD-11 Catatonia: Normative Modeling of Structural and Functional MRI Across Two Independent Cohorts.
item.description:
The American journal of psychiatry
Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome cutting across mood disorders (MODs) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). However, its neurobiological profiles remain poorly characterized. The authors examined structural and resting-state functional normative deviations associated with catatonia across two independent clinical cohorts, using hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling. Structural and resting-state functional MRI data were analyzed from two independent deeply phenotyped cohorts of 280 patients with MODs and SSDs. The Mannheim (Germany) sample included 184 patients with MODs or SSDs (58 with ICD-11 catatonia), and the Bern (Switzerland) sample comprised 96 SSD patients (59 with ICD-11 catatonia). Individual deviations from normative models were estimated using the PCNToolkit, based on healthy reference datasets (N=57,000 structural; N=22,000 functional). Catatonia diagnosis was associated with significant ventricular enlargement (third ventricle and left and right lateral ventricles; q<0.05) and cortical thinning in the left dorsal posterior cingulate and insular cortices (q<0.05) across both cohorts. Exploratory analyses identified a significant left orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) difference between MOD and SSD patients with catatonia. In the overall catatonia versus non-catatonia comparison, the OFC association survived false discovery rate correction only in models adjusted for demographic variables. Resting-state functional analyses showed reduced connectivity between sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and executive control networks at the nominal significance level, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. In the combined sample, catatonia was characterized by ventricular enlargement and cingulo-insular cortical thinning, supporting a transdiagnostic model implicating distributed motor-salience integration circuits. These findings provide reproducible, individual-level evidence for distributed brain network involvement in catatonia and identify candidate regions for future mechanistic and neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

item.title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease progression.
item.description:
Science advances
Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer's disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer's Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.
